title: Ibn al-Sammak and al-Rashid (తెలుగు)

full_text:
The Caliph Harun al-Rashid sat in his golden audience hall on a sweltering summer day, attended by emirs, viziers, and guards. The Caliph called for a drink, and a cupbearer brought him a crystal goblet filled with iced water scented with rose petals.

As the Caliph raised the goblet to his lips, an elderly, austere scholar named Ibn al-Sammak stepped forward and said: 'Hold, O Commander of the Faithful! Before you drink, permit me to ask you a single question.'

The Caliph paused and said: 'Speak, Ibn al-Sammak.'

The sage asked: 'If you were lost in the scorching wilderness of the desert, dying of thirst, and no man possessed water save one traveler with this single cup, what portion of your imperial kingdom would you give to obtain it?'

Harun al-Rashid replied without hesitation: 'By heavens, I would give half of my entire empire!'

The sage said: 'Drink, O Caliph, and may it be pleasant to your health.'

When the Caliph had drained the crystal goblet, the sage asked a second question: 'And if, through an affliction of the body, this water could not pass from your veins, causing you agonizing pain and threatening your life, what portion of your kingdom would you give to be relieved?'

The Caliph answered: 'I would give the remaining half of my empire!'

Ibn al-Sammak smiled with gentle philosophical authority: 'Then, O Commander of the Faithful, why do you boast of an empire whose total value in the balance of life is worth no more than a single cup of water and its release?'

Harun al-Rashid wept bitter tears of humility, recognized the fragility of earthly splendor, and treated the sage as his closest spiritual counselor.
moral: An entire empire of gold is worth less than a single cup of clear water in the hour of desperate thirst. [TE]
